raw_case_text: A 2-month-old boy was admitted to our hospital with purpura, bloody stools, and thrombocytopenia. His medical history included a recurrent skin rash, which first presented at birth. On admission, he was generally well, but had purpura and hepatosplenomegaly (liver: 2 cm below the right costal margin and spleen: 5 cm below the left costal margin). His platelet (PLT) count was 10 x 109 L-1, his hemoglobin level was 7.6 g/dL, and his leukocyte count was 15.9 x 109 L-1. His mean platelet volume (MPV) was 9.9 fL (normal range: 8.9-12.6 fL). Although a bone marrow examination revealed normal cellularity without any malignant cells, it did not reveal hypermegakaryocytes. Subsequently, an infectious laboratory workup was performed. An HCMV infection was confirmed because positivity for the specific antibody against HCMV immunoglobulin M and HCMV antigenemia (23 of 48,000 cells were positive) were detected. There was no laboratory evidence of a maternal cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection during pregnancy. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with ITP secondary to a CMV infection acquired after birth. An ophthalmic examination and audiogram produced normal findings. He received an intravenous infusion of immunoglobulins (IVIG: 1 g/kg/day) as a first-line therapy. Although the patient's PLT count temporarily rose (118 x 109 L-1) following the IVIG therapy, it gradually decreased to 10 x 109 L-1 within a week. Treatment with prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day) failed to improve the patient's PLT count, and repeated PLT transfusions were required. The intravenous administration of ganciclovir (10 mg/kg/day) was initiated for the CMV infection. Although no CMV antigenemia was present after 1 month, CMV antigenemia was seen again after the cessation of ganciclovir. Based on the patient's clinical course and the refractoriness of his condition to therapies targeting ITP and CMV antigenemia, WAS was strongly suspected. Flow cytometric (FCM) analysis revealed that the level of WAS protein (WASP) expression on the CD3-, CD19-, and CD56-positive cells from the patient was only 20% of that seen in the control (his father). Through direct DNA sequencing, we identified a novel missense mutation in exon 3 of the patient's WASP gene (c. 343 C > T, p. H115T; Figure 1). This mutation has not been described previously. The patient was diagnosed with WAS at 3 months after the onset of his condition. Subsequently, he underwent a cord blood transplant from an unrelated donor after receiving a conditioning regimen consisting of busulfan and cyclophosphamide. Ganciclovir was continued during the hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) until CMV antigenemia was no longer detected (Day 180). At present, the patient is 9 years old and well. His PLT count is within the normal range, and 100% donor engraftment was achieved.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-month-old boy presented with purpura, bloody stools, and severe thrombocytopenia on a background of a recurrent skin rash present since birth.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having experienced a recurrent eczematous skin rash since birth, the infant was admitted at 2 months of age with cutaneous purpura, hematochezia, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe thrombocytopenia (10 x 10^9/L) that proved refractory to IVIG, oral prednisolone, and ganciclovir therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recurrent skin rash since birth; no maternal history or laboratory evidence of gestational CMV infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cutaneous purpura, bloody stools, and recurrent skin rash since birth.

objective.physical_examination: Generally well-appearing infant with cutaneous purpura and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, spleen palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin). Ophthalmic examination and audiogram were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CBC: severe thrombocytopenia with platelets 10 x 10^9/L (transiently rising to 118 x 10^9/L after IVIG before relapsing to 10 x 10^9/L within 1 week), mean platelet volume (MPV) 9.9 fL (normal 8.9-12.6 fL), hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, and WBC 15.9 x 10^9/L. Serology was positive for human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) IgM, and peripheral blood HCMV pp65 antigenemia was positive (23 positive cells per 48,000 WBCs; cleared after 1 month of IV ganciclovir, recurred upon stopping ganciclovir, and cleared permanently by day +180 post-HSCT).
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow examination showed normal cellularity without malignancy or hypermegakaryocytosis. Flow cytometric analysis of CD3+, CD19+, and CD56+ lymphocytes demonstrated severely reduced Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) expression at 20% of normal control (paternal) levels. Direct DNA sequencing of the WAS gene identified a novel hemizygous missense mutation in exon 3: c.343C>T (p.H115Y / reported as p.H115T).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS; confirmed at 3 months after onset by 80% reduction in lymphocyte WASP expression on flow cytometry and a novel WAS exon 3 missense mutation c.343C>T) presenting initially at 2 months of age with postnatally acquired cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection and refractory severe thrombocytopenia/bloody stools (confirmed by positive HCMV IgM and HCMV antigenemia of 23/48,000 cells). Thrombocytopenia failed IVIG (1 g/kg/day) and prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day), and CMV antigenemia relapsed after initial 1-month IV ganciclovir (10 mg/kg/day). Curative unrelated umbilical cord blood transplantation (conditioned with busulfan and cyclophosphamide) with continuous peri-transplant IV ganciclovir through day +180 achieved permanent clearance of CMV antigenemia, 100% donor chimerism, normal platelet counts, and healthy survival at 9 years of age.
